description: Hi! I’m Matheus, a game dev from Brazil and indie studio founder. I recently shipped Sery: Into the World of Myths, a 2D pixel-art platformer on Steam. Strong technical background; I love game design and experimenting with new mechanics like computer vision and voice input. Join T-Minus to build a small, polished game we actually finish! Looking for: 2D artists (pixel art/animation), sound designers/composers, game designers/writers and programmers. Motivation over experience! 🚀
summary:
Ten Days on the Moon is a free browser game that trains kids aged 7 to 12 to think like mission engineers. The player runs a small outpost at the Moon's south pole for ten days. Each day they split a few energy cells between air and water, a greenhouse, a radiation shelter, a science lab and a battery, and walk the astronaut to a daily task. No choice is free: every cell spent in one place is missing somewhere else, and the cost shows up days later.

Real solar flares from NASA's DONKI catalog (with their real date and class, plus the particle events and coronal mass ejections DONKI links to them) decide how hard radiation hits the base, so protecting the crew competes with air, food and science. Every real fact in the game shows its NASA source and is labeled as archived data.

This answers the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge by turning a real engineering trade-off into a short loop a child can read and play, in English or Portuguese, with no download or account. The lesson a child should take away: on the Moon, energy is limited, and keeping the crew safe from the Sun costs energy you also need for everything else.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Ten Days on the Moon is a 3D mission trainer for kids aged 7 to 12 that runs in any web browser, with no download and no account. The player commands a small outpost at the Moon's south pole for ten days and has to bring the crew home safely.

HOW IT WORKS

Every day follows the same short loop: walk the astronaut to the day's task station, play a quick minigame, then return to the energy console and place the day's energy cells. Cells can go to Air and Water, the Greenhouse, the Radiation Shelter, the Science Lab or the Battery. Three meters tell the story: oxygen, radiation and battery. Oxygen at 0 or radiation at 10 ends the mission, and food runs out if the greenhouse is neglected.

Space weather is the pressure that makes the choices hard. The game ships 20 real solar flares curated from NASA's DONKI catalog (5 weak C-class, 10 medium M-class, 5 strong X-class, from 2017 to 2026). The real flare class decides how hard radiation hits the base. When DONKI links a coronal mass ejection to the flare, the crew gets a two-day warning; when it links a measured solar energetic particle event, the card shows it. After the event, a "This really happened" card shows the real date, class and source, labeled as archived data, never as live.

Daily events (moonquakes, micrometeorite hits, lunar dust, the cold of shadowed craters, water ice, Earth dipping below the horizon, sleep loss, homesickness, mold in the greenhouse) and daily tasks (communication delay, exercise, robotic arm capture) are each based on a NASA page that the card cites.

Two difficulty modes (Cadet and Commander) and two languages (English and Portuguese) make it usable in class and at home.

WHY IT MATTERS

Space-themed STEM content often hides the engineering trade-offs of a real mission. Here, no choice is free: every cell spent in one place is missing somewhere else, and the cost shows up days later. A child learns by doing that on the Moon energy is limited, and that protecting the crew from the Sun costs energy also needed for air, food and science. Using real, dated solar events shows that space weather is not made up, and the cited sources invite curious kids and teachers to read more.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

The game turns an abstract resource budget into a handful of energy cells a child can see, count and move. It never tells the player the right answer: it shows the consequence, then the real event behind it. A small robot pet, a readable low-sun polar landscape with long shadows and a black daytime sky, and short text cards keep a young player's attention without lowering the science.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Readability for ages 7 to 12 (short sentences, big icons, two languages); scientific honesty (every real fact has a NASA source, game values such as costs, chances and the 0 to 10 scales are labeled as game values, not measurements); no NASA logos or mission identifiers; and access (runs in a browser on modest school computers).

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

Unity 2022.3 (URP) with C#, exported to WebGL and hosted on itch.io. Game rules are written as plain C# with no engine dependency and covered by 209 automated EditMode tests. 3D models of the station and characters made in Blender. Python script to query and curate the DONKI FLR, SEP and CME catalogs; the raw JSON answers are kept unedited in the repository. Fonts: Barlow Semi Condensed and Nunito (SIL Open Font License). AI-assisted content: the game idea and design are the team's own. Parts of the C# code and tests were written with AI assistance (Claude) and reviewed by the team; concept boards and reference images were generated with AI (Gemini) and used as references to model in Blender, and any AI image shown carries a visible "AI-assisted" mark; some texts and translations were drafted with AI and reviewed. NASA data was not generated by AI. This is stated in the in-game credits, on the itch.io page and in USO-DE-IA.md in the repository.
